activities.anchor: the study of things that must not move
activities.caption: pair each half of the subject with its question
activities.name: ssHalvesMatch

config.prompt: Two questions organise the whole lesson — pair each half with its question:

pairs.right: what forces must each part carry? — equilibrium, rigid bodies
can the part survive carrying them? — stress, strain, bending, buckling, failure
statics treats every body as perfectly rigid; strength allows real deformations

config.why: Neither half is optional — a perfect force analysis of an inadequate beam still falls down, and an over-designed beam of unknown forces is guesswork with a budget.

activities.anchor: Real engineers never let the working point get near the crossing
activities.caption: pin the bridge live-load factor on the scale
activities.name: ssFactorPlace

config.prompt: Engineers multiply expected loads by a safety factor. About where do the factors for the live loads of bridges sit?
config.why: Roughly 1.5–2 on the live loads of bridges, about 1.5 for aircraft structure — much higher for cranes and anything lifting people; the failure zone sits outside anything the world delivers.

activities.anchor: combine like arrows, not like numbers
activities.caption: bet the resultant before the geometry
activities.name: ssVectorPredict

config.q: Two 50 N pulls act at right angles to each other. The resultant is about…
config.why: The diagonal of the right-angle pair is what the parallelogram rule gives — same-direction pulls would double it; perpendicular ones give √(50² + 50²) ≈ 71 N.

activities.anchor: That is why a door handle sits far from the hinges
activities.caption: pair each rotation idea with its picture
activities.name: ssMomentMatch

config.prompt: Moments and their kin — pair the quantity with its picture:

pairs.right: force times the perpendicular distance to the pivot
two equal, opposite forces on parallel lines — pure rotation, zero net push
snow on a roof, water on a dam — resultant acting at the centroid

config.why: Which is why the screwdriver turns the screw without shoving it across the table — pure rotation from a couple, no net push.

activities.caption: one line of the conversion slipped — find it
activities.name: ssUnitsSpot

config.prompt: A student converts a car's mass to weight. One line is wrong — click it:
lines: A car has a mass of 1,500 kg
The habit: estimate first — a tonne-scale mass weighs kilonewtons
config.correction: 1,500 N is a hundredth of the truth — a 1,500 kg car weighs about 15,000 N; when the magnitude disagrees with your estimate, stop and find the slip.
config.why: Kilograms measure matter, newtons measure force — the multiplication by g is a conversion you must do explicitly, every time.

config.prompt: The free-body diagram's drilled steps — put them in order:
items: Confirm the body is not accelerating — static equilibrium
Isolate one body and cut it free from the world
Draw every force: applied loads, weight, support reactions
config.why: A roller pushes perpendicular to its surface; a pin pushes in two directions; a fixed support also resists turning — and when you need one unknown out of the way, take moments about a pivot where its own moment is zero.

config.text: A 6 m simply supported beam carries a 600 N load 2 m from the left support. Moments about the left support: the right reaction times %%0%% m balances 600 N acting at %%1%% m, so it is %%2%% N; vertical balance gives the left reaction %%3%% N — the load did not split evenly.
config.hint: Take moments where one unknown's own moment is zero, then let ΣF = 0 hand you the rest.

activities.caption: normal or shear? file the loading
activities.name: ssStressBuckets

config.prompt: σ = F/A comes in two flavours — file each case:
buckets: normal stress — perpendicular to the cut
shear stress — parallel to the cut

items.label: tension through a thick rod — harmless
what bolts in a joint resist
the same force through a wire — brutal

config.why: Stress is the load spread over every square millimetre of the cut — and in the elastic region stress and strain are proportional, σ = E·ε: everything is a spring.
